exercises.objective: Explain the motivation for approximating a complicated distribution with a Gaussian.
exercises.prompt: Many distributions of practical interest (e.g. a Bayesian posterior over model parameters) are only known up to normalization, $p(x) = \frac1Z\tilde p(x)$ with $\tilde p$ easy to evaluate but $Z$ unknown and hard (recall PROB-04). Explain why approximating such a $p$ with a Gaussian, centered at $p$'s mode, is a useful strategy, even though $p$ generally isn't exactly Gaussian.
hints: A Gaussian is fully specified by just a mean and covariance, both cheap to work with (sample from, integrate against, combine with other Gaussians via PROB-05's identities), unlike an arbitrary unnormalized $\tilde p$.

Near its mode (highest point), a well-behaved unimodal distribution's log-density often looks locally quadratic, exactly the shape of a Gaussian's log-density, so a Gaussian can be a good LOCAL approximation even if $p$ isn't Gaussian globally.

Practically: this approximation sidesteps ever needing to compute the hard normalization constant $Z$ directly, the Gaussian approximation's own normalization is automatic (Gaussians always integrate to a known, closed-form value), trading an intractable exact answer for a cheap, often-good-enough approximate one.

exercises.objective: Derive the Laplace approximation from a second-order Taylor expansion of the log-density.
exercises.prompt: Let $x^*$ be the mode of $p(x)$ (so $\frac{d}{dx}\log p(x)\big|_{x^*}=0$). Using the second-order Taylor expansion of $\log p(x)$ around $x^*$ (from MATH-00, applied to $\log p$ instead of $p$ directly), show that $p(x)$ is approximately proportional to a Gaussian $N(x\mid x^*, \sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2 = \left(-\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\log p(x)\Big|_{x^*}\right)^{-1}$.
hints: Taylor-expand $\log p(x)$ to second order around $x^*$: $\log p(x) \approx \log p(x^*) + \left.\dfrac{d\log p}{dx}\right|_{x^*}(x-x^*) + \tfrac12\left.\dfrac{d^2\log p}{dx^2}\right|_{x^*}(x-x^*)^2$.

The linear term vanishes, since $x^*$ is the mode (the first derivative of $\log p$ is zero there, same as it being zero for $p$ itself). So $\log p(x) \approx \log p(x^*) + \tfrac12\left.\dfrac{d^2\log p}{dx^2}\right|_{x^*}(x-x^*)^2$.

Exponentiating: $p(x) \approx p(x^*)\exp\left(\tfrac12\left.\dfrac{d^2\log p}{dx^2}\right|_{x^*}(x-x^*)^2\right)$. Comparing to a Gaussian's exponent $-\dfrac{(x-x^*)^2}{2\sigma^2}$: matching gives $\dfrac{d^2\log p}{dx^2}\Big|_{x^*} = -\dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}$, i.e. $\sigma^2 = \left(-\left.\dfrac{d^2\log p}{dx^2}\right|_{x^*}\right)^{-1}$. Note the second derivative of $\log p$ at a mode is negative (it's a maximum), so this variance is correctly positive.

exercises.objective: Compute the Laplace approximation for a concrete unnormalized density.
exercises.prompt: Let $\log \tilde p(x) = -\tfrac14 x^4 + \tfrac12 x^2$ (unnormalized log-density). This has a mode at $x^*=1$ (you can verify $\tfrac{d}{dx}\log\tilde p\big|_{x=1} = -x^3+x\big|_{x=1}=0$). Compute the Laplace-approximation variance $\sigma^2$ at this mode. Enter a decimal.
